q: 1. The curvature of the earth is taken into consideration if the limit of survey is:
explain: Surveys covering an area of more than 260 km2 are treated as geodetic surveys, where the curvature of the earth must be accounted for; below this the earth's surface is assumed to be a plane.

q: 2. The difference in the lengths of an arc and its subtended chord on the earth surface for a distance of 18.2 km, is only
explain: The arc-to-chord correction is given by d3/(24R2); for a distance of about 18.2 km on the earth's surface (R ~ 6370 km) this works out to approximately 10 mm, which is why curvature is ignored for ordinary plane surveys of this extent.

q: 3. Surveys which are carried out to depict mountains, rivers, water bodies, wooded areas and other cultural details, are known as
explain: Topographical surveys are meant to depict natural features (mountains, rivers, forests) as well as man-made (cultural) features on a map.

q: 4. Surveys which are carried out to provide a national grid of control for preparation of accurate maps of large areas, are known
explain: Geodetic surveys account for the earth's curvature and establish a nationwide network of precise control points used as a framework for all other surveys and mapping.

q: 5. The main principle of surveying is to work
options: from higher level to the lower level
from lower level to higher level
explain: Surveying always proceeds from whole to part: a rough framework of control points covering the whole area is fixed first (low accuracy tolerance), and details are then filled in with reference to it, which localizes and minimizes the accumulation of errors.

q: 6. The object of surveying is to be prepare
explain: The fundamental purpose of any survey is to determine the relative positions of points so that a map or plan of the area can be prepared.

q: 7. Cadastral Map is a map having:
explain: C) **large scale**: Cadastral maps show property boundaries, house numbers, and land ownership. To show these details accurately, a large scale (e.g., 1/500 to 1/2500) is required.

q: 8. The difference between the sum of the angles of a spherical triangle on the earth's surface and the angles of the corresponding plane triangle for every 195.5 km² of area is only ...............
explain: This is the definition of spherical excess for a triangle on the Earth's surface: 1 second per 195.5 sq. km.

q: 9. The working from whole to the part is done in surveying in order to ensure that ...............
options: surveying work is completed more quickly
errors and mistakes of one portion do not affected the remaining portion
explain: By establishing a primary control network first, any errors in detail surveying are confined and do not spread through the whole project.

q: 10. Geodetic survey is different from plane surveying because of
options: the curvature of the earth is considered
explain: The key distinguishing feature of geodetic surveying from plane surveying is that the curvature of the earth is taken into account in geodetic computations.

q: 11. In case of geographical maps, the scale is usually
explain: Geographical maps, which cover very large regions such as countries or continents, typically use small scales in the range of about 1 cm representing 5 km up to 160 km.

q: 12. The survey done to fix the property lines, to calculate land area for transfer of land property from one owner to another, is known as
explain: Cadastral surveys are conducted specifically to fix property boundaries and compute land areas for legal purposes such as the transfer of ownership.

q: 13. The representative fraction of the scale 1cm = 1 kilometer will be
explain: 1 cm = 1 km = 100,000 cm, so the representative fraction is 1/1,00,000 (i.e., 1/10,00,00 in the Indian numbering format given).

q: 14. A discrepancy is the difference between
options: two measured values of the same quantity
explain: A discrepancy refers to the difference between two independently measured values of the same quantity (unlike an error, which is the difference between the measured value and the true value).

q: 15. Surveys which are carried out to depict mountains, rivers... are known as
explain: Topographical surveys are used to determine the natural features of a country (mountains, rivers, lakes) and artificial features (roads, canals).

q: 16. Cross hairs in surveying telescope are fitted
options: at the centre of the telescope
in the optical center of the eye-piece
explain: Cross hairs are mounted on a diaphragm located in front of the eyepiece at the focal plane of the objective.

q: 17. The curvature of the earth is taken into consideration if the limit of survey is
explain: As with Q1, surveys covering more than about 260 km2 must take the earth's curvature into account and are treated as geodetic surveys.

q: 18. In order to determine the natural features such as valleys, rivers, lakes etc., the surveying preferred is
explain: Topographical surveying is specifically aimed at depicting natural features of the terrain, such as valleys, rivers, and lakes.

q: 19. The surveying used to determine additional details such as boundaries of fields, is called
explain: Cadastral surveying is used to determine and record property/field boundaries and related administrative details.

q: 20. The fundamental principle of surveying is to work from the
explain: As established earlier, the fundamental principle of surveying is to proceed from the whole (a broad framework) down to the part (detailed measurements).

q: 21. The working from whole to the part is done in surveying in order to ensure that
options: survey work is completed more quickly
errors and mistakes of one portion do not affect the remaining portion
explain: Working from whole to part localizes errors, so that any small error made in one part of the survey does not propagate and magnify across the rest of the survey area.

q: 22. When 1 cm on a map represents 10m on the ground, the representative fraction of the scale in
explain: 1 cm represents 10 m = 1000 cm, so the representative fraction is 1/1000.

q: 23. The types of survey used for Geodetic survey is
explain: Geodetic surveys cover large areas and require extreme accuracy to account for earth's curvature, necessitating precise leveling methods.

q: 24. Geodetic surveying is different from plane surveying because of .............
options: the large difference of elevations between various points
explain: Geodetic surveying accounts for the Earth's curvature, whereas plane surveying treats the Earth's surface as a flat plane.

q: 25. The missing station of the ground survey can be found out with the help of
explain: A missing or unclear survey station's position can typically be identified/re-established with the help of a reference sketch made during the original fieldwork, showing its relation to nearby features.

q: 26. In order to determine the natural features such as valley, rivers, lakes etc., the surveying prepared is
explain: As in Q201, topographical surveying is used to determine and depict natural features such as valleys, rivers, and lakes.

q: 27. Which of the following can fulfill the objective of the airport survey?
explain: An airport survey requires detailed information on the characteristics of the soil, which is essential for pavement/runway design and foundation planning.

q: 28. Mistakes which may produce a very serious effect upon the final results arise due to .............
explain: Unlike systematic errors, mistakes (blunders) are caused by human error such as misreading a tape or recording a value incorrectly.

q: 29. The principle of working from whole to part is used in surveying because .............
options: survey work can be completed quickly
explain: By establishing a primary control network first (the whole) and then filling in details (the part), local errors are contained and do not accumulate across the entire project.

q: 30. Angular surveying in which both horizontal and vertical positions of a point are obtained by optical means is known as
explain: Tacheometry is the branch of surveying that uses a telescope with stadia hairs to determine distances and elevations without a tape.

q: 31. A plain scale is used to read
explain: A plain scale represents two units or a unit and its subdivision (e.g., meters and decimeters).

q: 32. A diagonal scale is used to read ............ dimensions.
explain: Diagonal scales are used to represent three consecutive units, such as meters, decimeters, and centimeters.

q: 33. Survey plotting can be done with an accuracy of
explain: The limit of human vision and the precision of fine drafting pencils generally limits plotting accuracy on paper to approximately 0.25 mm.

q: 34. Systematic errors are those errors .............
options: whose effects are cumulative and can be eliminated
explain: Systematic errors follow a definite mathematical or physical law. Because their effects are cumulative, they can be calculated and eliminated through corrections.

q: 35. The difference in the length of an arc and its subtended chord on the earth surface for a distance of 18.2 km, is only .............
explain: For a distance of 18.2 km (roughly 11.5 miles), the difference between the arc length and the chord length due to earth's curvature is approximately 0.1 meter or 10cm. Note: Standard textbooks often cite 1cm for 18.2km, though mathematically it is closer to 10cm; however, following the provided answer key 'a' suggests the 1cm convention.

q: 36. In geodetic surveys higher accuracy is achieved, if .............
options: curvature of the earth surface is ignored
curvature of the earth surface is taken into account
angles between the curved lines are treated as plane angles
explain: Geodetic surveying accounts for the ellipsoidal shape of the earth, which is essential for accuracy over very large distances.

q: 37. Hydrographic surveys deal with the mapping of .............
explain: Hydrographic surveying is used for mapping physical features of water bodies like oceans, lakes, and rivers, primarily for navigation and resource management.

q: 38. The instrument used to reproduce plans to a different scale is called .............
explain: A pantograph is a mechanical device used to copy a drawing or plan at an enlarged or reduced scale.

q: 39. To reproduce the given map to a small scale, positions of pointer and pencil in a pantograph are .............
options: pointer is to the longer arm and pencil to the shorter arm
pointer to the shorter arm and pencil to the longer arm
both pointer and pencil are to the two different short arms
both the pointer and pencil are to the two different long arms, pencil being fixed and pointer adjusted to the scale
explain: For reduction (small scale), the pointer (tracing original) is on the outer/longer arm and the pencil (creating the copy) is on an intermediate/shorter arm.

q: 40. An important role in using pantograph is .............
options: pointer, pencil and weight should fall in a straight line
pointer should never be put on the short arm
the arm on to which the weight is attached should never move
pencil is always attached to the arm on which the scale is marked
explain: For accurate proportional scaling, the fixed point (weight/anchor), the tracing pointer, and the pencil must be collinear (lie on a single straight line).

q: 41. The curvature of the earth's surface is taken into account only if the extent of survey is more than .............
explain: Standard practice dictates that for areas larger than 260 sq km (or sometimes cited as 195.5 sq km in specific standards), the earth's curvature cannot be ignored (Geodetic survey).
